items.title: Agriculture in the Economy & Cropping Seasons
items.body:
**In one line** — Farming feeds and employs most of India yet produces a shrinking slice of national output, and its year is split into three sowing seasons.

**Why it is asked** — APPSC loves the gap between jobs and output (~45% of workers, ~18% of output) and the Kharif/Rabi/Zaid season-and-crop pairs.

## The story

- **GVA** (Gross Value Added) is simply the value of all goods and services produced. Agriculture and allied sectors contribute close to one-fifth — about **18% of GVA/GDP** — but give work to roughly **45-46% of all workers**, and **over 58% of rural households** live off it.
- Because so many people share so little output, **output per farm worker is low** — economists call the surplus labour on farms **disguised unemployment** (people who look employed but add almost nothing to output).
- Over the decades agriculture's **share of GDP has fallen** (money and jobs shifted to services) even though the *amount* of food grown kept rising. This shift from farming to services is called **structural transformation**.
- **India's world ranks (2024):** the world's **largest producer of total milk** and **first in total pulses**, and the **largest exporter of rice** — but in **wheat India is second** (China is the largest producer).
- About **52% of cultivated land is rainfed** (watered only by rain, not canals or borewells), so a weak monsoon still hurts output.

## Cropping seasons

| Season | Sowing | Harvest | Major crops |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Kharif** | Jun-Jul (monsoon) | Sep-Oct | Rice, maize, cotton, bajra, jowar, groundnut, soybean |
| **Rabi** | Oct-Dec (winter) | Mar-May | Wheat, barley, gram, mustard, peas |
| **Zaid** | Mar-Jun (summer) | Jun-Aug | Short-duration summer crops: watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber, fodder |

- **Kharif** needs heat plus heavy rain; **Rabi** needs a cool growing spell then warm ripening; **Zaid** are short summer crops that need assured irrigation.

## Terms explained

- **GVA** — value added by producers; GDP = GVA + taxes − subsidies.
- **Rainfed** — farmland watered only by rainfall.
- **Disguised unemployment** — extra workers on a farm whose removal would not cut output.

**Don't confuse** — *Kharif* (sown with the June monsoon, rice) with *Rabi* (sown in winter, wheat). Hook: Kha**r**if = **r**ains; Rabi = winte**r** harvest in spring.

**Remember it** — Agriculture is a big employer but a small (and shrinking) earner.

**TL;DR**

| Point | Value |
|---|---|
| Share of GVA | ~18% |
| Share of workforce | ~45-46% |
| Rural households dependent | >58% |
| Rainfed cropland | ~52% |
| Seasons | Kharif (rains), Rabi (winter), Zaid (summer) |
keyPoints: Agriculture is ~18% of GVA but employs ~45-46% of the workforce; >58% of rural households depend on it.
Agriculture's GDP share has fallen over time as services grew (structural transformation).
About 52% of India's cultivable land is rainfed, making output monsoon-dependent.
Kharif = monsoon crops (rice, cotton) sown Jun-Jul; Rabi = winter crops (wheat, gram) sown Oct-Dec; Zaid = short summer crops (watermelon).
items.mnemonic: Seasons by weather: Kharif = rains, Rabi = winter, Zaid = summer.

items.title: Green Revolution & Coloured Revolutions
items.body:
**In one line** — The Green Revolution made India self-sufficient in foodgrains, and later 'colour' revolutions did the same for milk, fish, oilseeds and more.

**Why it is asked** — Match-the-colour questions and the Swaminathan–Borlaug link are near-certain; the drawbacks feed Mains answers.

## The story

- After the mid-1960s food crisis India launched the **Green Revolution** (from about 1965) to grow more foodgrain fast.
- The method was a package: **HYV seeds** (high-yielding variety seeds that give far more grain per plant) **+ chemical fertilisers + assured irrigation + double-cropping** (two crops a year on the same land).
- **M.S. Swaminathan** is regarded as its father in India, drawing on **Norman Borlaug's** HYV wheat from Mexico. Early gains were concentrated in **wheat and rice**, especially in **Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh**.
- Result: India became **self-sufficient in foodgrains** — but at a cost: **falling groundwater, soil-nutrient loss, heavy chemical use, higher input costs and regional imbalance** (the east and dryland crops were left behind).
- Swaminathan's later idea, the **Evergreen Revolution**, means raising output *without* harming the ecology.

## Coloured revolutions

| Revolution | Product |
|---|---|
| Green | Foodgrains (wheat, rice) |
| White (Operation Flood) | Milk |
| Blue | Fisheries |
| Yellow | Oilseeds / edible oil |
| Pink | Meat / prawn |
| Golden | Horticulture / honey |
| Silver | Eggs / poultry |
| Golden Fibre | Jute |

- The **Rainbow Revolution** denotes the integrated, holistic development of agriculture together with all its allied 'colour' revolutions — it encompasses the Green (foodgrains), White (milk), Blue (fisheries) and Yellow (oilseeds) revolutions, among others. Its aim is to make agriculture as a whole more productive, profitable and sustainable.

## Terms explained

- **HYV seeds** — specially bred seeds that yield much more grain, but need more water and fertiliser.
- **Operation Flood** — the 1970s dairy programme (Verghese Kurien, Amul model) behind the White Revolution.
- **Double-cropping** — growing two crops in a year on the same field.

**Don't confuse** — *White* = milk and *Blue* = fish (not the reverse); *Yellow* = oilseeds, not fish.

**Remember it** — Colour matches the product: milk is White, water (fish) is Blue, cooking oil is Yellow.

**TL;DR**

- Green Revolution (post-1965): HYV seeds + fertiliser + irrigation; Swaminathan (with Borlaug), wheat/rice in Punjab-Haryana.
- Drawbacks: groundwater and soil depletion, costs, regional imbalance → answered by the Evergreen Revolution.
- White=milk, Blue=fish, Yellow=oilseeds, Pink=meat/prawn, Golden=honey/horticulture; Rainbow = all together.
keyPoints: Green Revolution (post-1965) used HYV seeds, fertiliser and irrigation; M.S. Swaminathan (with Borlaug's work) led it in India.
Early Green Revolution gains were in wheat/rice in Punjab, Haryana and western UP.
Drawbacks: groundwater and soil depletion, higher costs, regional imbalance.
White = milk (Operation Flood, Kurien); Blue = fish; Yellow = oilseeds; Pink = meat/prawn; Golden = honey/horticulture.

items.title: Land Reforms & Holding Categories
items.body:
**In one line** — After 1947 India tried to give land to those who till it and to stop a few people owning too much.

**Why it is asked** — The 'four planks', the Bhoodan name-and-year, and the hectare size-classes are classic one-mark facts.

## The story

Post-Independence land reform had four main planks:

1. **Abolition of intermediaries** — the old **zamindars** (landlords who collected rent for the British but did not farm) were removed, and ownership went to the actual cultivators.
2. **Tenancy reforms** — state laws to protect tenants' rights and cap the rent they pay.
3. **Land ceilings** — a legal maximum on how much land one family may hold; the surplus is redistributed.
4. **Consolidation of holdings** — merging a farmer's scattered small plots into one block to cut **fragmentation**.

- Alongside these came **cooperative farming** and the **Bhoodan Movement** (**1951**, led by **Acharya Vinoba Bhave**) in which landlords voluntarily gifted land; the **first donation was by V. Ramachandra Reddy** (Pochampally, Telangana).
- **Small Farmer Large Field (SFLF)** — many small/marginal farmers keep their own plots but organise into groups to synchronise and harmonise selected agricultural operations (sowing the same variety, buying inputs, spraying, selling together), so they get the scale benefits of one large field. It is **not** a government takeover or corporate leasing.
- More recently, NITI Aayog's **Model Agricultural Land Leasing Act, 2016** makes renting land legal and lets tenant-farmers get bank credit.

## Holding categories

| Size | Class |
|---|---|
| less than 1 ha | Marginal |
| 1-2 ha | Small |
| 2-4 ha | Semi-medium |
| 4-10 ha | Medium |
| more than 10 ha | Large |

- **Marginal + small holdings together are over 85% of all holdings**, so the average farm is tiny — a core reason for low farm incomes.

## Terms explained

- **Zamindar** — a landlord-intermediary who collected rent but did not cultivate.
- **Tenant** — a farmer who tills land owned by someone else and pays rent.
- **Fragmentation** — one farmer's land split into many small scattered plots.
- **Land ceiling** — the legal maximum area a family may own.

**Don't confuse** — *Tenancy reform* (protects renters) with *land ceiling* (caps ownership) — both exist, but they do different jobs. India never **nationalised** farmland — there was no nationalisation of all agricultural land by the Union government; that is a common wrong option.

**Remember it** — "Bhoodan = Bhave" (both start with B), 1951, Pochampally.

**TL;DR**

- Four planks: abolish intermediaries, regulate tenancy, impose ceilings, consolidate holdings (+ cooperative farming).
- Bhoodan 1951, Vinoba Bhave; first donor V. Ramachandra Reddy.
- Size classes: less than 1 ha Marginal, 1-2 Small, 2-4 Semi-medium, 4-10 Medium, more than 10 Large.
- Model Land Leasing Act 2016 legalises leasing and tenant credit; farmland was never nationalised.
keyPoints: Land reforms had four planks: abolition of intermediaries, tenancy regulation, land ceilings, consolidation (plus cooperative farming).
Bhoodan Movement (1951) led by Acharya Vinoba Bhave; first land donation by V. Ramachandra Reddy.
Land classes: <1 ha marginal, 1-2 ha small, 2-4 ha semi-medium, 4-10 ha medium, >10 ha large.
Model Agricultural Land Leasing Act, 2016 (NITI Aayog) legitimises leasing and tenant credit access.

items.title: MSP, CACP & Cost Concepts
items.body:
**In one line** — MSP is a government-promised floor price for crops, worked out from the farmer's cost of production.

**Why it is asked** — Who recommends vs approves, the 23-crop basket, the A2/A2+FL/C2 cost ladder and the Swaminathan C2+50% formula are perennial favourites.

## The story

- The **Minimum Support Price (MSP)** is a price announced *before* sowing. If the market price crashes, government agencies buy the crop at the MSP, so the farmer is protected. It began in **1965-66** with the Green Revolution and was **first announced for wheat (1966-67)**.
- It is **recommended** by the **Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP)** — set up in **1965 as the Agricultural Prices Commission (APC)** and **renamed CACP in 1985** — and then **approved by the Cabinet (CCEA)**. CACP recommends, Cabinet decides.
- MSP is announced for **23 crops** (including **niger**, a Kharif oilseed).
- **Sugarcane is different**: it gets a **Fair and Remunerative Price (FRP)** approved by the **Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA)** (CACP only recommends); states may add a higher **State Advised Price (SAP)**.
- Produce is sold in markets run under each **State's APMC Act**; **e-NAM (2016)** is the all-India online mandi platform.

## The 23 crops

- **7 cereals** (paddy, wheat, barley, jowar, bajra, maize, ragi), **5 pulses** (gram, arhar, moong, urad, lentil), **7 oilseeds**, **4 commercial** (cotton, sugarcane [FRP], raw jute, copra).

## Cost concepts (the cost ladder)

| Cost | Includes |
|---|---|
| **A2** | Paid-out costs only — seeds, fertiliser, irrigation, hired labour |
| **A2+FL** | A2 + the value of the family's own labour (FL) |
| **C2** | A2+FL + imputed rent and interest on the farmer's own land and capital |

- The **Swaminathan Commission** (National Commission on Farmers) urged MSP at least **50% above the C2 (comprehensive) cost** — C2 + 50%; the government instead uses **A2+FL + 50%** (a lower base).
- Who buys at MSP: **FCI** (foodgrains), **NAFED** (pulses/oilseeds), **CCI** (cotton).
- **Problems:** buying is skewed to **Punjab/Haryana/MP**, farmer **awareness is low (~23%)**, few crops are covered, it pushes water-hungry paddy/wheat, and it strains the budget.

## Terms explained

- **MSP** — a pre-announced floor price the government promises to pay.
- **Imputed cost** — a cost you do not pay in cash but that still counts (your own land's rent, your family's labour).
- **FRP / SAP** — the sugarcane floor price set by the Centre (FRP) and the extra a state may add (SAP).

**Don't confuse** — CACP **recommends** MSP; the **CCEA (Cabinet) approves** it. And MSP is **not legally guaranteed** — it is a policy price, not a right.

**Remember it** — Cost ladder A2 → A2+FL → C2 = "paid cash → add family labour → add owned-asset rent".

**TL;DR**

- MSP since 1965-66, first for wheat (1966-67); CACP (APC 1965 → CACP 1985) recommends, CCEA approves; 23 crops.
- Sugarcane = FRP (CCEA), states may add SAP; markets run under State APMC Acts; e-NAM 2016.
- A2 (cash) → A2+FL (+family labour) → C2 (+owned rent/interest); Swaminathan C2+50% vs govt A2+FL+50%.
- Procurement: FCI foodgrains, NAFED pulses/oilseeds, CCI cotton; 2026-27 common paddy MSP = ₹2,441/quintal.
keyPoints: MSP introduced 1965-66; recommended by CACP, announced for 23 crops (7 cereals, 5 pulses, 7 oilseeds, 4 commercial).
MSP first announced for wheat (1966-67); CACP began as the Agricultural Prices Commission (APC) in 1965, renamed CACP in 1985.
Sugarcane gets a Fair and Remunerative Price (FRP) approved by the CCEA (CACP recommends); States may add a State Advised Price (SAP).
Farm produce is regulated under State-enacted APMC Acts; e-NAM (2016) is the pan-India electronic mandi platform; niger is a Kharif oilseed under MSP.
A2 = paid-out costs; A2+FL adds family labour; C2 adds imputed rent/interest on owned assets.
Swaminathan Commission recommended MSP = C2 + 50%; government uses A2+FL+50%.

MSP is criticised for regional skew, low awareness and encouraging water-guzzling paddy/wheat.

items.title: Farmer-Welfare Schemes & Institutional Credit
items.body:
**In one line** — A set of central schemes puts money, insurance, water and markets within a farmer's reach, backed by a rural-credit system led by NABARD.

**Why it is asked** — Scheme-to-purpose matching (KUSUM, e-NAM, PMFBY, PM-KISAN) and 'who is the apex rural-credit body' are high-frequency.

## Key schemes

| Scheme | Year | Focus |
|---|---|---|
| **PM-KISAN** | 2018/19 | ₹6,000/year income support (three ₹2,000 instalments via DBT); disbursal ongoing (20th instalment in Aug 2025) |
| **PMFBY** | 2016 | Crop insurance launched in 2016 replacing the earlier NAIS and Modified NAIS schemes; uniform farmer premium 2% Kharif / 1.5% Rabi / 5% commercial/horticultural crops; voluntary since 2020, even for loanee farmers |
| **PM Kisan Maan Dhan** | 2019 | ₹3,000/month pension for small farmers after 60 |
| **Soil Health Card** | 2015 | Nutrient-status advisory for each field |
| **PMKSY** | 2015 | Irrigation potential & water efficiency ('per drop, more crop') |
| **KUSUM** | 2019 | Solar-powered irrigation pumps |
| **e-NAM** | 2016 | Online national agri-market linking mandis |
| **PKVY** (Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana) | 2015 | Organic farming in farmer clusters |
| **BPKP** (Bharatiya Prakritik Krishi Paddhati) | 2020 | Chemical-free natural farming (a sub-scheme of PKVY) |

- **DBT** (Direct Benefit Transfer) means money is paid straight into the farmer's bank account, cutting out middlemen.

## Institutional credit

- **NABARD** (National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development, **1982**) is the **apex** body that **refinances** rural and farm credit — it lends to the banks that lend to farmers.
- Credit reaches farmers through **commercial banks, cooperatives and Regional Rural Banks (RRBs)**.
- The **Kisan Credit Card (KCC, 1998)** gives a farmer a ready short-term crop loan. Farm lending is a **priority-sector** target (banks must lend a set share to agriculture).

## Terms explained

- **DBT** — benefit paid directly into a bank account.
- **Refinance** — NABARD lends to banks so they can on-lend to farmers.
- **Priority-sector lending** — RBI rule forcing banks to lend a fixed share to farms and small units.

**Don't confuse** — *PM-KISAN* (₹6,000 income support) with *PM Kisan Maan Dhan* (₹3,000/month pension after 60) — same 'Kisan' name, different schemes.

**Remember it** — NABARD is the 'bank of banks' for the village; the KCC is the farmer's crop-loan card.

**TL;DR**

- PM-KISAN (2018/19): ₹6,000/year in 3 DBT instalments (ongoing; 20th in Aug 2025).
- PMFBY (2016): insurance, premiums 2%/1.5%/5%, voluntary for loanee farmers since 2020.
- KUSUM = solar pumps, Soil Health Card = nutrient advice, PMKSY = irrigation, e-NAM = online market.
- NABARD (1982) apex refinancer; KCC (1998) short-term crop loans; credit via banks, cooperatives, RRBs.

items.title: Food Security, NFSA & the Andhra Pradesh Angle
items.body:
**In one line** — India grows enough grain, but turning that into real nutrition for all is the job of the NFSA and the PDS — and Andhra Pradesh adds its own farm strengths and schemes.

**Why it is asked** — NFSA entitlements, the FAO four dimensions, and AP's shrimp/horticulture/irrigation facts are all directly examinable, including the AP-specific angle APPSC prizes.

## The story — food security

- The **FAO** (UN Food and Agriculture Organization) says food security has **four dimensions: Availability, Accessibility, Utilization and Stability** (not 'affordability', a common trap).
- The **National Food Security Act (NFSA), 2013** gives **5 kg of foodgrain per person per month** to **priority households** and **35 kg per household** to **Antyodaya (AAY)** families. It covers **75% of rural + 50% of urban people (about 67% — two-thirds — roughly 813 million)**; households are entitled to these quantities by law.
- For a ration card, the **eldest woman aged 18 or above is treated as the head of the household**. **Pregnant and lactating women** get a **maternity benefit (₹6,000)** and a **take-home ration (~600 kcal, 18-20 g protein per day under ICDS norms)**.
- Grain reaches people through the **PDS/TPDS** (ration shops); **One Nation One Ration Card (ONORC)** lets a migrant draw rations anywhere; **PMGKAY** distributes additional/free foodgrains to NFSA beneficiaries (free since Jan 2023). **FCI** holds the buffer stock and buys at MSP.
- Despite record foodgrain output, a large share of Indians remains undernourished (**about 195 million**), with high child stunting and anaemia — because high production does not automatically ensure economic and physical access to a balanced, nutritious diet (*availability* alone does not guarantee *access* and *utilization*).

## The story — Andhra Pradesh

- **Rice** is the major food crop, irrigated largely by the **Krishna and Godavari** rivers (also the Penna and Tungabhadra); the Krishna-Godavari delta is AP's **'rice bowl'**.
- AP is India's **largest shrimp producer (~70%)** and a top exporter of Vannamei shrimp; it has India's **second-longest coastline**.
- In horticulture AP ranks first in the country in the area and production of **oil palm and papaya**, and **1st in chillies, cocoa, lime and tomato** (2nd in cashew, mango, sweet orange). Farming engages about **60% of AP's people**.
- AP's **Annadata Sukhibhava** (one of the state's 'Super Six' promises) is a farmer income-support (investment support) scheme designed to work alongside and supplement the Centre's PM-KISAN; it was allocated about **₹6,600 crore in the 2026-27 State Budget**.
- **Rythu Bharosa Kendras (RBKs)** are village-level one-stop centres offering quality seeds, fertilisers, advisory services and procurement support.
- Both are **state** (AP) initiatives, not Union schemes applied uniformly across all states.
- AP's all-round push across crops and allied sectors is dubbed the **Rainbow Revolution**.

## AP irrigation projects (status as of 2026)

| Project | Source river / key feature | Status / target (2026) |
|---|---|---|
| **Polavaram** | Multipurpose national project on the Godavari river; accorded **National Project status** by the Central Government; its **Right Main Canal** is designed to link Godavari waters towards the Krishna basin | Civil works targeted for completion around **March 2027**; commissioning targeted before the **2027 Godavari Pushkarams**; hydroelectric units **not yet** operational |
| **Pattiseema Lift Scheme** | Lifts surplus Godavari water into the Polavaram Right Main Canal to serve the Krishna delta, interlinking the Godavari and Krishna rivers | Working; an AP scheme, **not** part of the national Ken-Betwa link |
| **Handri-Neeva Sujala Sravanthi** | Longest canal carrying Srisailam (Krishna) water to drought-prone Rayalaseema | Lift/canal scheme for Rayalaseema |
| **Galeru-Nagari** | Lift/canal scheme chiefly aimed at drought-prone Rayalaseema | Under construction |
| **Poola Subbaiah Veligonda** | Tunnels Srisailam (Krishna) water to fluoride/drought areas of Prakasam, Nellore and Kadapa | Phase-1 directed to be completed by **mid-2026** |
| **Godavari-Banakacherla link** | Proposed inter-basin transfer of Godavari water south | **Proposed; under inter-state/environmental scrutiny** — not commissioned |

**Don't confuse** — Pattiseema (a quick *lift* that already moves Godavari water to the Krishna delta) with Polavaram (the big *dam* still being completed).

## Terms explained

- **Priority / AAY households** — the two NFSA groups; AAY (Antyodaya) are the poorest, getting a fixed 35 kg per family.
- **PDS/TPDS** — the ration-shop network delivering subsidised/free grain.
- **Buffer stock** — grain FCI stores to steady prices and meet shortages.

**Don't confuse** — The FAO fourth dimension is **Stability**, not **Affordability**. And **Annadata Sukhibhava** is a *state* scheme that *tops up* the central *PM-KISAN*.

**Remember it** — Food-security four = A-A-U-S (Availability, Accessibility, Utilization, Stability).

**TL;DR**

- FAO four dimensions: Availability, Accessibility, Utilization, Stability.
- NFSA 2013: 5 kg/person (priority), 35 kg/household (AAY), ~67% of people; eldest woman (18+) = head; take-home ration ~600 kcal.
- ONORC = portable card; PMGKAY = free grain via FCI buffer stock; ~195 million still undernourished.
- AP: largest shrimp producer (~70%), 1st in chillies/oil palm/papaya; Annadata Sukhibhava (₹6,600 cr) via RBKs; Polavaram before 2027 Pushkarams.

Pregnant/lactating women get maternity benefit (₹6,000) and a take-home ration of ~600 kcal (18-20 g protein) under ICDS norms.
ONORC makes ration cards portable; PMGKAY gives free foodgrains via FCI buffer stocks.
AP is India's largest shrimp producer (~70%) with the second-longest coastline; India is the world's largest rice exporter.
AP ranks 1st in chillies, cocoa, lime, oil palm, papaya and tomato; rice bowl in the Krishna-Godavari delta.

AP farmer welfare: Annadata Sukhibhava (₹6,600 cr, Budget 2026-27) via Rythu Bharosa Kendras; key projects Polavaram (before 2027 Pushkarams), Handri-Neeva, Galeru-Nagari, Veligonda, Pattiseema; 'Rainbow Revolution'.

items.title: Types of Agriculture, Plan Record, Latest Output & Leading States
items.body:
**In one line:** agriculture has many branches (each with a "-culture" name), a Plan-by-Plan growth record, and a set of record output numbers and leading states that examiners love to pair.

**Why it is asked:** "match the culture with the activity", "which Plan saw negative farm growth" and "India's rank / top state" are one-mark staples.

## Branches of agriculture (the "-cultures")

**The story**

| Term | Activity |
|---|---|
| **Sericulture** | Silk production by rearing **silkworms** |
| **Moriculture** | Growing **mulberry** plants (food for silkworms) |
| **Apiculture** | **Beekeeping** for honey and wax |
| **Viticulture** | **Grapes** (especially for wine) |
| **Pisciculture** | **Fish** breeding and rearing |
| **Aquaculture** | Fish, shellfish and algae in controlled water |
| **Vermiculture** | Rearing **earthworms** for compost |
| **Floriculture** | **Flowers** and ornamental plants |
| **Aviculture** | Raising **birds** |
| **Arboriculture** | **Trees** and shrubs |
| **Horticulture** | Fruits, vegetables, flowers and ornamental plants |

- Agriculture covers about **43%** of India's geographical area.
- Agriculture's GDP share (source text): **19.9% (2020-21)**, 19% (2021-22) and **18.3% (2022-23)**.

## Agriculture in the Five-Year Plans

| Plan | Point | Farm growth |
|---|---|---|
| **First (1951-56)** | Food crisis; **14%** of outlay to agriculture | 2.71% |
| Second (1956-61) | Share cut to **11.7%**; industry first | 3.17% |
| **Third (1961-66)** | Introduced **IADP** and **HYVP**; **negative growth** | **-0.73%** |
| Sixth (1980-85) | **Second Green Revolution (1983-84)** | 4.3% |
| **Eighth (1992-97)** | Good weather — best Plan growth | **4.68%** |
| Tenth (2002-07) | National Agricultural Policy for sustainable growth | 2.3% |
| Eleventh (2007-12) | Missed the **4%** target | 3.6% |

- Annual farm growth: **6.6% (2017-18)**, 2.1% (2018-19), 5.5% (2019-20), 3.3%, 3.0% and **3.5% (2022-23)**.

## Latest output (2025-26)

- **Foodgrain** output 2025-26 (third advance estimates, May 2026): a record **376.56 million tonnes**, with wheat about **121 million tonnes**.
- **Horticulture** output 2025-26: a record about **377.8 million tonnes** — now larger than foodgrain output.
- In **January 2026** India became the **world's largest rice producer**, overtaking **China** (Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan); India is also the largest **rice exporter**.

## India's world ranks (source table, 2024)

| Rank | Products |
|---|---|
| **1st** | Total **milk**, total **pulses**, **jute** |

items.title: MSP Numbers, PM-AASHA, Price Terms, Committees & Marketing Reforms
items.body:
**In one line:** beyond "CACP recommends, CCEA approves", the exam asks the latest MSP figures, the PM-AASHA components, the price terms, the farm-policy committees and the 2017-2022 marketing reforms.

**Why it is asked:** MSP announcements are current affairs every season; UPSC 2018 (which crops get MSP), UPSC 2020 (what moves rice prices) and UPSC 2023 (niger) test precision.

## Latest MSP / FRP

**The story**

| Price | Season | Value (₹/quintal) |
|---|---|---|
| **Paddy (common)** MSP | Kharif Marketing Season **2026-27** (CCEA, 13 May 2026) | **2,441** (+₹72); Grade A **2,461** |
| **Wheat** MSP | Rabi Marketing Season **2027-28** (CCEA, 30 Sep 2026) | **2,610** (+₹25 — smallest rise in 17 years) |
| **Sugarcane FRP** | Sugar season **2026-27** | **365** (+₹10 over ₹355) |

- In the 2027-28 rabi round the highest absolute rise was for **safflower (₹675)**.
- The **CACP** also weighs **terms of trade** between farm and non-farm sectors, **inter-crop price parity**, demand-supply and the effect on consumers.

## PYQ precision

- **UPSC 2018:** MSP is announced for **barley, finger millet (ragi), groundnut and sesamum** — **not** for areca nut, coffee or turmeric.
- **UPSC 2023:** **Niger** (Guizotia abyssinica) is a **Kharif** oilseed with an MSP, and some **tribal** people use niger oil for cooking.
- **UPSC 2020:** the price of rice is shaped by **MSP, government trading, government stockpiling and consumer subsidies** — all four.

## Price terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Procurement price** | Price at which government actually buys (historically above MSP) |
| **Central Issue Price (CIP)** | Subsidised price at which grain is issued under the PDS |
| **PM-AASHA (2018)** | Umbrella of **Price Support Scheme (PSS)**, **Price Deficiency Payment Scheme (PDPS)** and **Pilot of Private Procurement & Stockist Scheme (PPPS)** |

- Under **PDPS** the farmer is paid the **difference between MSP and the market price** instead of physical buying.

## Committees

| Committee | Year | Remembered for |
|---|---|---|
| **Swaminathan — National Commission on Farmers (NCF)** | **2004-06** | MSP = C2 + 50%; led to the **National Policy for Farmers, 2007** |
| **Shanta Kumar High Level Committee** | **2014** (report 2015) | Restructure **FCI**; only about **6%** of farmers sell at MSP to procurement agencies; cut NFSA coverage to about **40%** |
| **Ashok Dalwai Committee** | **2016** | Strategy for **Doubling Farmers' Income** |
| **MSP Committee (Sanjay Agrawal)** | **July 2022** | Set up after the farm-law repeal to make MSP more effective |

## Marketing reforms

- **Essential Commodities Act, 1955** — lets government control stocks and prices of essential goods.
- **e-NAM** — launched **14 April 2016**; lead agency **SFAC** (Small Farmers' Agribusiness Consortium).
- **Model APLM Act, 2017** (Agricultural Produce and Livestock Marketing) and **Model Contract Farming Act, 2018** — templates for States.
- **Three farm laws (September 2020)** were **repealed** by the **Farm Laws Repeal Act, 2021** (announced 19 November 2021).

**Don't confuse** — *PSS* (government buys the crop) with *PDPS* (government pays only the price gap). And *Shanta Kumar* (FCI restructuring, 2014) with *Dalwai* (doubling income, 2016).

**TL;DR**
- Paddy 2026-27 ₹2,441; wheat 2027-28 ₹2,610 (+₹25); sugarcane FRP 2026-27 ₹365; safflower biggest rise ₹675.
- MSP covers barley, ragi, groundnut, sesamum, niger — not areca nut, coffee, turmeric.
- PM-AASHA 2018 = PSS + PDPS + PPPS; CIP = PDS issue price.
- NCF 2004-06; Shanta Kumar 2014 (6% farmers); Dalwai 2016; MSP committee 2022.
- ECA 1955; e-NAM 14 April 2016 (SFAC); APLM 2017; contract farming 2018; farm laws repealed 2021.

items.title: Green Revolution History, BGREI, Every Coloured Revolution & Allied Sectors
items.body:
**In one line:** the Green Revolution grew out of famine and food-aid dependence, was pushed by named people and programmes, and was followed by a long list of "colour" revolutions for allied sectors.

**Why it is asked:** names (C. Subramaniam, Borlaug, Kurien, Pitroda), programmes (PL-480, IADP, HYVP, BGREI) and the full colour list are direct one-mark questions.

## Before the Green Revolution

- The **Bengal Famine of 1943** killed about **2-3 million** people.
- Under the US **PL-480 ("Food for Peace", 1954)** programme India imported large amounts of **wheat** — a dependence that pushed India towards self-sufficiency.
- **IADP** (Intensive Agricultural District Programme, **1960-61**) and the **HYVP** (High Yielding Varieties Programme, **1966-67**) were the launch pads.

## Green Revolution — people and seeds

**The story**

| Who / what | Point |
|---|---|
| **Norman Borlaug** | Developed dwarf HYV **wheat** in Mexico; **Nobel Peace Prize 1970** |
| **M.S. Swaminathan** | Scientist who led it in India |
| **C. Subramaniam** | Union **Agriculture Minister** — the political architect |
| **IR-8** | HYV **rice** from IRRI (Philippines) |

- **BGREI** (Bringing Green Revolution to Eastern India) began in **2010-11** under the **RKVY**, for Assam, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Odisha, eastern UP and West Bengal; food-grain growth there was **11.99%** in 2011-12.
- The **Second Green Revolution** stresses the **eastern states**, organic and **contract farming**, **APMC Act amendments**, drought-proof crops and cold chains.

## Every coloured revolution

| Revolution | Product |
|---|---|
| Green | Foodgrains |
| **White** (Operation Flood) | Milk |
| **Blue** | Fish |
| **Yellow** | Oilseeds / edible oil — **Sam Pitroda**; Technology Mission on Oilseeds (**1986**) |
| **Pink** | Prawns and meat processing (some books add onion) |
| **Silver** | Eggs and poultry |
| **Golden** | Honey (source); horticulture in many books |
| **Golden Fibre** | **Jute** |
| **Silver Fibre** | **Cotton** |
| **Grey** | **Fertilisers** |
| **Round** | **Potato** |
| **Red** | Meat and tomato |
| **Brown** | Leather and cocoa |

| Other "revolution" | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Evergreen** | Swaminathan — more output without ecological harm |
| **Rainbow** | Announced in **2000** (National Agriculture Policy) for **4%** farm growth |
| **Tricolour** | Coined by PM Modi — **Saffron (energy)**, White and Blue |
| **Operation Greens** | Budget 2018 (Arun Jaitley) — **tomato, onion, potato (TOP)** |
| **Sweet** | Scientific beekeeping under the **National Beekeeping and Honey Mission** |

## Allied sectors

- **Operation Flood** began in **1970** under the **NDDB** (founded **1965**, **Anand**, Gujarat), led by **Verghese Kurien**.
- **Uttar Pradesh** is India's largest **milk**-producing state.
- **PMMSY** (Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana, **2020**, ₹20,050 crore) drives the Blue Revolution.

**Don't confuse** — *Golden Fibre* = jute but *Silver Fibre* = cotton; *Silver* = eggs; *Grey* = fertilisers; *Round* = potato.

**TL;DR**
- Bengal Famine 1943; PL-480 wheat 1954; IADP 1960-61; HYVP 1966-67.
- Borlaug (Nobel 1970), Swaminathan, C. Subramaniam; IR-8 rice.
- BGREI 2010-11 under RKVY (eastern states, 11.99% growth 2011-12).
- Silver Fibre cotton, Golden Fibre jute, Grey fertiliser, Round potato, Yellow oilseeds (Pitroda, 1986).
- Rainbow 2000; Operation Greens TOP (2018); Sweet = honey mission; Operation Flood 1970, NDDB 1965 Anand; UP top milk; PMMSY 2020.
keyPoints: Bengal Famine of 1943 killed about 2-3 million people.
PL-480 (Food for Peace, 1954) supplied US wheat to India before the Green Revolution.
IADP began in 1960-61 and the HYVP in 1966-67.
Norman Borlaug won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970; C. Subramaniam was the Agriculture Minister behind the Green Revolution; IR-8 was the HYV rice from IRRI.
BGREI began in 2010-11 under the RKVY for eastern states; foodgrain growth there was 11.99% in 2011-12.
The Second Green Revolution stresses eastern states, organic and contract farming and APMC Act amendments.
Yellow Revolution (oilseeds) is linked to Sam Pitroda and the Technology Mission on Oilseeds (1986).
Golden Fibre = jute; Silver Fibre = cotton; Silver = eggs; Grey = fertilisers; Round = potato; Red = meat and tomato; Brown = leather and cocoa.
Rainbow Revolution was announced in 2000 for 4% farm growth; Tricolour = Saffron (energy), White and Blue.
Operation Greens (Budget 2018) covers tomato, onion and potato (TOP); Sweet Revolution = National Beekeeping and Honey Mission.
Operation Flood began in 1970 under the NDDB (1965, Anand) led by Verghese Kurien; Uttar Pradesh is the largest milk-producing state.
PMMSY (2020, ₹20,050 crore) drives the Blue Revolution.
Green Revolution drawbacks included groundwater depletion, soil-nutrient loss and regional imbalance.

items.title: Farm Inputs — Seeds, Fertiliser Policy, Natural Farming, Irrigation & Land Records
items.body:
**In one line:** every input — seed, fertiliser, water, soil advice and land title — has its own law, policy or scheme with a year.

**Why it is asked:** "which year / which scheme" pairs (NBS 2010, neem-coated urea, PPV&FR 2001, Sikkim organic) recur in state PSC papers.

## Seeds

**The story**

| Law / policy | Year |
|---|---|
| **Seeds Act** | **1966** |
| **Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights (PPV&FR) Act** | **2001** |
| **National Seeds Policy** | **2002** — tackles the low **seed replacement rate** |

## Fertilisers

| Policy | Year | Point |
|---|---|---|
| **Nutrient Based Subsidy (NBS)** | **2010** | Fixed subsidy per nutrient for **P and K** fertilisers (urea excluded) |
| **New Urea Policy** | **2015** | Energy-efficient domestic urea production |
| **Neem-coated urea** | **2015** | Made **100%** mandatory to stop diversion |
| **Nano urea** (IFFCO) | **2021** | Liquid urea; first plant at **Kalol**, Gujarat |
| **One Nation One Fertiliser** | **2022** | Single brand **"Bharat"**; PM Kisan Samriddhi Kendras |
| **PM-PRANAM** | **2023** | Rewards States that cut chemical-fertiliser use |

## Organic and natural farming

- **PKVY** (2015) — cluster-based **organic** farming; **BPKP** (2020) — chemical-free natural farming.
- **National Mission on Natural Farming (NMNF)** — approved **25 November 2024** with **₹2,481 crore**.
- **Sikkim** was declared India's **first fully organic state** in **2016**.

## Water and soil

- **PMKSY** (**2015**) — "**Har Khet Ko Pani**" and "**Per Drop More Crop**"; **drip** irrigation saves water and fertiliser, **sprinklers** suit high-density crops.
- **Soil Health Card** — launched **19 February 2015** at **Suratgarh** (Rajasthan).
- **NFSM** (National Food Security Mission, **2007**) — more rice, wheat and pulses by area expansion and productivity.

## Land records and holdings

- **NLRMP** (**2008**) merged **Computerisation of Land Records (CLR)** with **Strengthening of Revenue Administration and Updating of Land Records (SRA&ULR)**; it is now the **DILRMP** (Digital India Land Records Modernisation Programme), moving towards **conclusive titles**.
- **Agriculture Census 2015-16:** average holding **1.08 hectare**; small and marginal farms are about **86%** of holdings.
- The **Kumarappa Committee (1949)** on agrarian reforms recommended "land to the tiller".

**Don't confuse** — *NBS* covers phosphatic and potassic fertilisers; **urea** stays under a separate fixed-price regime.

**TL;DR**
- Seeds Act 1966; PPV&FR 2001; National Seeds Policy 2002.
- NBS 2010; New Urea Policy and 100% neem-coated urea 2015; nano urea 2021 (Kalol); Bharat brand 2022; PM-PRANAM 2023.
- PKVY 2015, BPKP 2020, NMNF Nov 2024 (₹2,481 cr); Sikkim first organic state 2016.
- PMKSY 2015 (Har Khet Ko Pani, Per Drop More Crop); Soil Health Card 2015 Suratgarh; NFSM 2007.
- NLRMP 2008 (CLR + SRA&ULR) → DILRMP; average holding 1.08 ha; Kumarappa 1949.

New Urea Policy 2015; neem-coated urea made 100% mandatory in 2015.
IFFCO nano urea launched in 2021, first plant at Kalol (Gujarat).
One Nation One Fertiliser (2022) uses the single brand 'Bharat'; PM-PRANAM (2023) rewards States cutting chemical fertilisers.
National Mission on Natural Farming approved 25 November 2024 with ₹2,481 crore.
Sikkim was declared India's first fully organic state in 2016.
PMKSY (2015): 'Har Khet Ko Pani' and 'Per Drop More Crop'.
Soil Health Card scheme launched 19 February 2015 at Suratgarh, Rajasthan.
NFSM launched in 2007 for rice, wheat and pulses.
NLRMP (2008) merged CLR and SRA&ULR; now DILRMP, aiming at conclusive titles.

items.title: Farm Credit, Crop Insurance, PM-KISAN 2026 & the New Missions
items.body:
**In one line:** farm credit grew out of named committees (AIRCS, CRAFICARD, R.V. Gupta), insurance moved to PMFBY, and 2024-26 added a wave of missions for pulses, oilseeds, natural farming and backward farm districts.

**Why it is asked:** committee-to-institution pairs, the KCC limit, the PMFBY updates and the new missions' outlays are prime current affairs.

## Credit — committees and institutions

**The story**

| Committee | Year | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| **All India Rural Credit Survey (A.D. Gorwala)** | **1951-54** | Imperial Bank → **State Bank of India (1955)** |
| **CRAFICARD (B. Sivaraman)** | **1979** | Recommended **NABARD**, set up **12 July 1982** |
| **R.V. Gupta Committee** | **1998** | **Kisan Credit Card** |
| **Vaidyanathan Committee** | **2004** | Revival of short-term rural **cooperative** credit |

- Short-term cooperative credit is **three-tier**: **PACS** (village) → **DCCB** (district) → **StCB** (state).
- **Commercial banks** give the **largest share** of institutional farm credit.
- **Interest subvention:** crop loans at **7%**, with a **3%** prompt-repayment incentive — effective **4%**.
- **Budget 2025-26** raised the KCC loan limit under the Modified Interest Subvention Scheme to **₹5 lakh**; KCC was extended to **animal husbandry and fisheries** in 2018-19.
- **UPSC 2020 (KCC):** short-term KCC credit can cover **working capital for maintenance of farm assets**, **post-harvest expenses** and **consumption** needs of farm households.
- **UPSC 2020 (public investment):** **computerisation of PACS**, **social capital** development and **cold storage** built by government count as **public investment** in agriculture — MSP fixing, free power and loan waivers do not.

## Insurance

- **PMFBY** was launched on **18 February 2016** at **Sehore** (Madhya Pradesh), replacing **NAIS (1999)** and **MNAIS**.
- It covers **post-harvest losses** (up to 14 days) from **cyclones and unseasonal rain** (UPSC 2016).
- From **Kharif 2026** it also covers losses from **wild animal attacks** and **paddy inundation**.

## PM-KISAN in 2026

- Launched **24 February 2019** at **Gorakhpur** (effective from 1 December 2018); fully **Central** funding.
- The **23rd instalment** was released in **June 2026**.
- On **31 July 2026** the Cabinet approved its **continuation from 2026-27 to 2030-31** with **₹3.15 lakh crore**.

## New missions

| Mission | Approved | Key numbers |
|---|---|---|
| **PM Dhan-Dhaanya Krishi Yojana** | **July 2025** | **100** low-productivity districts; **₹24,000 crore a year** for **6 years**; converges **36** schemes |
| **Mission for Aatmanirbharta in Pulses** | **1 October 2025** | **₹11,440 crore**, **2025-26 to 2030-31**; tur, urad and masoor |
| **National Mission on Edible Oils — Oilseeds** | **October 2024** | **₹10,103 crore**, to 2030-31 |
| **NMEO — Oil Palm** | **August 2021** | ₹11,040 crore; focus on the North-East and Andaman |
| **Digital Agriculture Mission** | **September 2024** | **₹2,817 crore**; **AgriStack** farmer IDs |

**Don't confuse** — CRAFICARD (1979) recommended NABARD; the **R.V. Gupta** committee gave the KCC; **Gorwala**'s survey led to SBI.

**TL;DR**
- AIRCS (Gorwala) 1951-54 → SBI 1955; CRAFICARD (Sivaraman) 1979 → NABARD 1982; R.V. Gupta 1998 → KCC; Vaidyanathan 2004.
- PACS-DCCB-StCB; commercial banks largest; 7% loans, 3% prompt bonus = 4%; KCC ₹5 lakh (Budget 2025).
- PMFBY 18 Feb 2016, Sehore; post-harvest cover; wild animals and paddy inundation from Kharif 2026.
- PM-KISAN 24 Feb 2019 Gorakhpur; 23rd instalment June 2026; extended to 2030-31 (₹3.15 lakh crore).
- PM-DDKY 100 districts ₹24,000 cr/yr; pulses ₹11,440 cr; oilseeds ₹10,103 cr; digital agriculture ₹2,817 cr.

items.title: PDS Evolution, Nutrition Data, Agri Institutions & AP Agriculture 2025-26
items.body:
**In one line:** the PDS evolved in steps into the NFSA and free grain under PMGKAY; a set of named institutions and boards runs farm policy (several in Andhra Pradesh); and AP's own farm support was rebuilt in 2024-26.

**Why it is asked:** PDS years, GHI rank, board headquarters and AP's Annadata Sukhibhava / APCNF facts are recurring APPSC items.

## PDS → NFSA → PMGKAY

**The story**

| Step | Year |
|---|---|
| **Revamped PDS (RPDS)** — remote and hilly areas | **1992** |
| **Targeted PDS (TPDS)** — BPL / APL two-tier prices | **1997** |
| **Antyodaya Anna Yojana (AAY)** — poorest families | **2000** |
| **NFSA** — priced at **₹3** rice, **₹2** wheat, **₹1** millets per kg | **2013** |

- **Global Hunger Index 2025:** India **102nd of 123** ("serious").

items.title: For Mains — Agriculture & Allied Sectors
items.body:
**In one line** — For Mains Paper-IV, agriculture is argued as a development-and-welfare question: how to lift farm incomes and nutrition sustainably, with Andhra Pradesh as the live case.

**Why it is asked** — Syllabus clauses M4-7 (agricultural development — GDP share, Green Revolution, MSP, Swaminathan, Rainbow Revolution) and M4-8 (AP agriculture — irrigation disparities, horticulture/fisheries/dairy, schemes).

## The dimensions Mains asks

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| **Significance** | ~18% of GVA but ~45% of jobs and >58% rural livelihoods; food & raw-material security; demand base for industry |
| **Causes of distress** | Tiny fragmented holdings (85%+ marginal/small), ~52% rainfed, price volatility, thin credit reach, groundwater and soil stress |
| **Policy response** | MSP/CACP, PM-KISAN, PMFBY, e-NAM, KCC/NABARD, natural farming (BPKP), FPOs |
| **Limitations** | MSP's regional skew (Punjab/Haryana/MP) and low ~23% awareness; cereal-centric food security; crop-pattern bias to water-guzzlers |
| **Way forward** | Diversify to pulses/millets/horticulture/allied; income-plus-insurance support; micro-irrigation; climate-resilient and natural farming |

## Data, committees and schemes to quote

- **Swaminathan Commission (NCF):** MSP = **C2 + 50%** (government uses A2+FL+50%).
- **23 MSP crops**; 2026-27 common paddy MSP **₹2,441/quintal**.
- **NFSA 2013** covers ~67% (813 million); India **102nd of 123** on the **Global Hunger Index 2025** — the self-sufficiency vs nutrition gap.
- **SDG-2 (Zero Hunger)** by 2030; doubling-farmers'-income goal.

## The AP angle

- Largest **shrimp** producer (~70%); horticulture leader (chillies, oil palm, papaya); allied sectors (fisheries, dairy, horticulture) are the high-value growth engine.
- Irrigation disparities: canal-rich coastal delta vs drought-prone **Rayalaseema** (Handri-Neeva, Galeru-Nagari); **Polavaram** keystone; **Annadata Sukhibhava** + **RBKs** as the delivery model.

## Use in answers

- **Example:** contrast Punjab's MSP-paddy lock-in with AP's diversification into aquaculture to argue for crop-pattern reform.
- **Quote:** M.S. Swaminathan — "If agriculture goes wrong, nothing else will have a chance to go right."
- **Diagram idea:** a simple flow — *inputs (seed/water/credit) → production → MSP/market → income → nutrition* — and mark where each scheme intervenes.

**TL;DR** — Frame agriculture as income + nutrition + sustainability; quote Swaminathan C2+50%, NFSA, GHI 2025 (102/123); use AP aquaculture-and-horticulture diversification and Rayalaseema irrigation gaps as the case study.

Way forward: diversify to allied/horticulture/millets, income-plus-insurance, micro-irrigation, climate-resilient natural farming.
